newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan urges Japanese restraint over islands.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan urges Japanese restraint over islands.

text.p: Taiwan's Foreign Ministry expressed "grave concern" on Tuesday over a visit by a Japanese legislator to the disputed Diaoyu islands in the East China Sea, and urged Japan to exercise restraint.
"We urge Japan to exercise self-restraint and not to create any trouble that will affect our friendly relations," Foreign Ministry spokesman Roy Wu told a news conference.
"The Republic of China government reiterates its sovereignty over the Diaoyu Islands. This position is unquestionable," Wu said.
Wu said Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government hoped to resolve the sovereignty row through peaceful means.
The disputed East China Sea archipelago is claimed by Taipei, Beijing and Tokyo.

Shingo Nishimura, a conservative member of Japan's main opposition New Frontier Party, and three other people landed on the Senkaku Islands, known in Chinese as the Diaoyus, on Tuesday to inspect security and hold a brief commemorative ceremony.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was quick to distance the central government from Nishimura's group, which included former cabinet minister Shintaro Ishihara. He is the author of the 1980s nationalist treatise "A Japan That Can Say No".
Government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said that while the islands were Japanese territory, the group's actions were "extremely regrettable" and should not be allowed to damage Japan-China relations.
China's foreign ministry assailed the latest landing on the Diaoyus, calling it a serious violation of China's territorial sovereignty.
"The Chinese side expresses its strong indignation and opposition," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing.
"The Diaoyu islands have been a part of Chinese territory since ancient times," Shen said.

The cluster of uninhabited islands has ignited fiery nationalist passions in Chinese communities in Hong Kong and Taiwan since a Japanese right-wing group built a makeshift lighthouse there last July.
In the months that followed, the lighthouse drew a flotilla of vessels carrying Taiwanese and Hong Kong Chinese protesters, several of whom landed briefly on the islands.
Last September, a Hong Kong activist drowned when he jumped into stormy waters near the islands to press China's claim.
In February, Japan sent a letter to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan in which it sought to have Tokyo's position on the islands included in a U.N. report on the law of the sea.
Japan took the islands as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895 and refuses to acknowledge that the dispute is open for discussion with China or Taiwan.
China and Taiwan say the islands have been Chinese territory for centuries and should have been returned after Japan's defeat in World War Two.
